title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
This notebook shows common dimensions of SS Swagelok tubing and estimates steady-state heat conducted down the length of a 316 stainless steel tube, from a warm end to a cold end. Often times in cryogenic gas systems, SS tubing is used to traverse a cryostat from room temperature down to cryogenic temperatures. Estimating the heat load can be useful to figure out if you need more tubing length or a smaller diameter to reduce heat loads on the cryostat, or if you need more tubing volume you can figure out how much additional heat load you might apply to the cryostat.
Here we use the NIST cryogenic thermal-conductivity curve fit for the specific metal. NIST has some great publications and a resources on cryogenic properties of common materials. Solids are accessible on the website, and liquids/gases can be accessed through the RefProp software package, which is similar to CoolProp.


Code
#Load all of the libraries
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import quad

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
Tubing Geometric Data
Often times, when designing or operating low volume gas handling systems, knowing the volume per unit length of tube can be useful. This section reads the tubing data for Swagelok 316SS tubing (Tabel 3 - Fractional Stainless Steel Seamless Tubing), adds tubing volume (cc) per inch length and inch length per unit volume (cc). Calcuating volume (cc) per inch length is as simple as multiplying the tube cross-section by the unit conversion cubed.
\[\frac{Vol [cc]}{Len [in]} = \frac{\pi \cdot (OD[in] - 2*thk[in])^2}{4} \cdot (2.54\frac{[cm]}{[in]})^3\]


Code
from fractions import Fraction
tubes = pd.read_csv("SwagelokTubeSizes.csv", header=[0, 1])
#tubing volume per inch of length
#tubing length per cc of volume
tubes[("vol_len","cc/in")] = np.pi/4*(tubes[("Tube_OD","in")] - 2*tubes[("Wall","in")])**2 * (2.54)**3
tubes[("len_vol","in/cc")] = 1/tubes[("vol_len","cc/in")]
tubes[("Tube_OD","in")] = tubes[("Tube_OD","in")].apply(lambda x: Fraction(x).limit_denominator(16))
tubes.round(3)

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
1. NIST thermal-conductivity correlation
Type 316 stainless steel: - Temperature (T): kelvin (K) - Thermal conductivity (k(T)): W/(m·K) - NIST measured-data range: 4–300 K
NIST source: Material Properties: 316 Stainless Steel
The curve fit is expressed as:
\(log_{10}(k)=a+bX+cX^2+dX^3+eX^4+fX^5+gX^6+hX^7+iX^8\)
where \((X=log_{10}(T))\), with (\(T\)) in kelvin and (\(K\)) in \(W/(m·K)\).
The coefficients below are transcribed from the NIST 316 stainless steel curve fit. Use the correlation within the NIST measured-data range of 4–300 K for engineering calculations.


Code
# NIST Type 316 stainless steel thermal conductivity coefficients
NIST_K_COEFFS = {
    "a": -1.4087,
    "b":  1.3982,
    "c":  0.2543,
    "d": -0.6260,
    "e":  0.2334,
    "f":  0.4256,
    "g": -0.4658,
    "h":  0.1650,
    "i": -0.0199,
}

T_MIN_K = 4.0
T_MAX_K = 300.0

def k_316ss(T_K):
    """NIST 316SS thermal conductivity in W/(m K), valid for 4 <= T <= 300 K."""
    T = np.asarray(T_K, dtype=float)
    if np.any(~np.isfinite(T)) or np.any(T < T_MIN_K) or np.any(T > T_MAX_K):
        raise ValueError(f"Temperature must be between {T_MIN_K:g} and {T_MAX_K:g} K.")
    x = np.log10(T)
    c = NIST_K_COEFFS
    log10_k = (c["a"] + c["b"]*x + c["c"]*x**2 + c["d"]*x**3
               + c["e"]*x**4 + c["f"]*x**5 + c["g"]*x**6
               + c["h"]*x**7 + c["i"]*x**8)
    result = 10**log10_k
    return float(result) if result.ndim == 0 else result

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(T_plot, k_316ss(T_plot))
plt.xlabel("Temperature (K)")

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
3. Tube geometry and end temperatures
Physical model: one-dimensional, steady-state axial conduction through the metal annular cross-section of a straight tube. The two ends are held at specified temperatures. The model assumes no heat exchange with the surroundings along the tube, no parallel heat paths through fittings/supports, and constant tube dimensions.
Edit the inputs below.

tube_od_in: tube outside diameter, inches
wall_thickness_in: wall thickness, inches
tube_length_m: axial length between the warm and cold ends, metres
T_warm_K, T_cold_K: temperatures at the two ends, kelvin

The metal cross-sectional area conducting heat axially is the annular area:
\(A_m=\frac{\pi}{4}(D_o^2-D_i^2)\)
where \((D_i=D_o-2t)\). This is not the fluid-flow area inside the tube.


Code
# -------- USER INPUTS: EDIT THESE VALUES --------
tube_od_in = 0.1250           # tube outside diameter, inches
wall_thickness_in = 0.028    # wall thickness, inches
tube_length_m = 0.5          # axial distance between warm and cold ends, metres
T_warm_K = 38.0             # warm-end temperature, kelvin
T_cold_K = 4.0              # cold-end temperature, kelvin
# ------------------------------------------------

IN_TO_M = 0.0254

if tube_od_in <= 0 or wall_thickness_in <= 0:
    raise ValueError("OD and wall thickness must be positive.")
if 2 * wall_thickness_in >= tube_od_in:
    raise ValueError("Wall thickness leaves no positive internal diameter.")
if tube_length_m <= 0:
    raise ValueError("Tube length must be positive.")
if T_warm_K == T_cold_K:
    raise ValueError("Warm- and cold-end temperatures must differ.")
if not (T_MIN_K <= T_warm_K <= T_MAX_K and T_MIN_K <= T_cold_K <= T_MAX_K):
    raise ValueError("Both end temperatures must be within the NIST 4–300 K data range.")

tube_id_in = tube_od_in - 2*wall_thickness_in
Do_m = tube_od_in * IN_TO_M
Di_m = tube_id_in * IN_TO_M
metal_area_m2 = np.pi/4 * (Do_m**2 - Di_m**2)

print(f"Tube OD: {tube_od_in:.4f} in")
print(f"Tube ID: {tube_id_in:.4f} in")
print(f"Metal cross-sectional area: {metal_area_m2:.6e} m²")
print(f"Axial length: {tube_length_m:.4g} m")
print(f"End temperatures: {T_warm_K:.2f} K and {T_cold_K:.2f} K")

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
4. Axial heat conduction calculation
For a straight tube with constant metal cross-sectional area and temperature-dependent conductivity:
\(\dot Q=\frac{A_m}{L}\int_{T_c}^{T_h} k(T)\,dT\)
where:

\((\dot Q)\) = steady-state axial heat-transfer rate [W]
\((A_m)\) = metal annular cross-sectional area [m²]
\((L)\) = axial tube length between the two temperature boundaries [m]
\((k(T))\) = thermal conductivity [W/(m·K)]
\((T_h,T_c)\) = warm- and cold-end temperatures [K]

The integral is evaluated numerically. The reported heat leak is a positive magnitude, flowing from the warm end toward the cold end.


Code
T_low = min(T_warm_K, T_cold_K)
T_high = max(T_warm_K, T_cold_K)

integral_k_dT, integration_error = quad(
    lambda T: k_316ss(T),
    T_low,
    T_high,
    epsabs=1e-9,
    epsrel=1e-8,
)

Qdot_W = (metal_area_m2 / tube_length_m) * integral_k_dT

axial_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Metal cross-sectional area",
        "Integrated conductivity, ∫k(T)dT",
        "Axial heat leak for entered tube length",
        "Axial heat leak per meter of tube",
        "Numerical integration error estimate",
    ],
    "Value": [
        metal_area_m2,
        integral_k_dT,
        Qdot_W,
        Qdot_W / tube_length_m,
        integration_error,
    ],
    "Units": [
        "m²",
        "W/m",
        "W",
        "W/m²",
        "W/m",
    ],
})

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
5. Axial temperature profile
For steady axial conduction with no heat entering or leaving the tube along its length, the heat rate is constant. The temperature profile is generally nonlinear because (k) changes with temperature.
The profile below is calculated by inverting the cumulative integral of (k(T)).


Code
n_points = 200
x_m = np.linspace(0, tube_length_m, n_points)

# Cumulative integral of k(T) from the cold-end temperature to each temperature.
T_dense = np.linspace(T_low, T_high, 5000)
k_dense = k_316ss(T_dense)
cum_k = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(0.5 * (k_dense[1:] + k_dense[:-1]) * np.diff(T_dense))])

# The cumulative integral fraction varies linearly with axial position.
position_fraction = x_m / tube_length_m
if T_cold_K < T_warm_K:
    target_integral = position_fraction * cum_k[-1]
    T_profile = np.interp(target_integral, cum_k, T_dense)
else:
    target_integral = (1 - position_fraction) * cum_k[-1]
    T_profile = np.interp(target_integral, cum_k, T_dense)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(x_m, T_profile)
plt.xlabel("Distance from cold end (m)")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (K)")
plt.title("Steady-state axial temperature profile along 316SS tube")
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Swagelok SS316 Tubing - Some Useful Data
text:
6. Important assumptions and limitations

Axial conduction only: This estimates heat conducted through the tube metal along its length. It does not calculate radial conduction through the wall.
No distributed heat exchange: The tube is assumed thermally isolated along its length. If the tube is exposed to ambient air, radiation, insulation, or intermediate thermal anchors, the temperature profile and heat leak will change.
End temperatures: The inputs are metal temperatures at the two ends, not necessarily fluid temperatures. Fluid-to-wall convection or boiling resistance is outside this model.
Parallel paths: Fittings, valves, weldments, supports, braids, and other connected metal paths are excluded.
Geometry: Nominal dimensions and constant cross-sectional area are assumed. Thermal contraction is neglected.
Material properties: The correlation is for reference Type 316 stainless steel. Actual properties can vary with composition, processing, and cold work.
Property range: The notebook restricts temperatures to the NIST 4–300 K measured-data range.

For a long tube exposed to ambient surroundings or with intermediate thermal intercepts, a segmented model with distributed heat input/removal is more appropriate.

Cryogenic Joint Analysis: Universal Through-Bolt vs. Blind-Tapped Configurator
text:
This notebook models temperature-dependent joint dynamics from 293.15 K down to 4 K. Adjust the geometry dictionary settings and re-run to analyze.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import quad






Code
def get_nist_copper_alpha(T):
    """Exact NIST log-log polynomial for C10100 / OFHC Copper CTE (1/K)."""
    T = max(T, 4.0)
    a, b, c, d = -17.9081289, 67.131914, -118.809316, 109.9845997
    e, f, g = -53.8696089, 13.30247491, -1.30843441
    log10_T = np.log10(T)
    log10_y = (a + b * log10_T + c * log10_T**2 + d * log10_T**3 + 
               e * log10_T**4 + f * log10_T**5 + g * log10_T**6)
    return (10**log10_y) * 1e-6

def get_c10100_properties(T, T_ref=293.15):
    """Returns E (Pa) and dL/L for C10100 Copper via NIST Monograph 177."""
    E_GPa = 137.0 - 1.27e-4 * (T**2)
    dL_L, _ = quad(get_nist_copper_alpha, T_ref, T)
    return E_GPa * 1e9, dL_L

def get_ss316_properties(T, T_ref=293.15):
    """Returns E (Pa) and dL/L for SS316 via NIST Polynomials."""
    if T >= 23.0:
        le_105 = -2.9554e2 - 3.9811e-1 * T + 9.2683e-3 * T**2 - 2.0261e-5 * T**3 + 1.7127e-8 * T**4
    else:
        le_105 = -300.04
    dL_L = le_105 * 1e-5
    
    if T >= 48.0:
        E_GPa = 2.079488e2 + 7.394241e-2 * T - 9.627200e-4 * T**2 + 2.845560e-6 * T**3 - 3.240800e-9 * T**4
    else:
        E_GPa = 2.084729e2 - 1.358965e-1 * T + 8.368629e-3 * T**2 - 1.381700e-4 * T**3 + 6.831930e-7 * T**4
    return E_GPa * 1e9, dL_L

def get_molybdenum_properties(T, T_ref=293.15):
    """Returns E (Pa) and dL/L for pure Molybdenum via NIST Polynomials."""
    T = max(T, 4.0)
    a, b, c, d, e = -90.912613, -0.127173, 0.00266801, -5.0432E-06, 3.5183E-09
    dL_L_105 = a + b*T + c*(T**2) + d*(T**3) + e*(T**4)
    E_GPa = 329.0 - 0.038 * (T - 293.15)
    return E_GPa * 1e9, dL_L_105 * 1e-5

def get_material_properties(mat_name, T, T_ref=293.15):
    """Unified factory routing for properties extraction with clean tuple unpacking."""
    name = mat_name.upper()
    if name in ['SS316', 'STAINLESS', 'BOLT']:
        return get_ss316_properties(T, T_ref)
    elif name in ['C10100', 'COPPER', 'CU']:
        return get_c10100_properties(T, T_ref)
    elif name in ['MOLYBDENUM', 'MOLY', 'MO']:
        return get_molybdenum_properties(T, T_ref)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown material name indicator: {mat_name}")







Code
def calculate_frustum_stiffness(z1, z2, d_w, d_h, E, alpha_deg=30.0):
    """Computes stiffness for an isolated member frustum layer according to Shigley."""
    if np.isclose(z1, z2): return float('inf')
    alpha = np.radians(alpha_deg)
    tan_a = np.tan(alpha)
    num = (2 * z2 * tan_a + d_w - d_h) * (2 * z1 * tan_a + d_w + d_h)
    den = (2 * z2 * tan_a + d_w + d_h) * (2 * z1 * tan_a + d_w - d_h)
    return (np.pi * E * d_h * tan_a) / np.log(num / den)

def get_grip_length(geom):
    """Helper to find total physical clamp height based on joint type architecture."""
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
        return geom['t_w1'] + geom['t_p1'] + (0.5 * geom['L_eng'])
    else:
        return geom['t_w1'] + geom['t_p1'] + geom['t_p2'] + geom.get('t_w2', 0.0)

def get_member_stiffness(geom, T):
    """Dispatches stiffness stack tracking based on specified structural boundaries."""
    d_w, d_h = geom['d_w'], geom['d_h']
    t_w1, t_p1 = geom['t_w1'], geom['t_p1']
    
    E_w1, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T)
    E_p1, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T)
    E_p2, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T)
    
    compliance = 0.0
    
    # --- CONFIGURATION A: BLIND TAPPED HOLE ---
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
        t_p2_eff = 0.5 * geom['L_eng']
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, t_w1, d_w, d_h, E_w1)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1, t_w1 + t_p1, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1 + t_p1, t_w1 + t_p1 + t_p2_eff, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
        
    # --- CONFIGURATION B: THROUGH-BOLT & NUT ---
    else:
        t_w2, t_p2 = geom.get('t_w2', 0.0), geom['t_p2']
        L_grip = t_w1 + t_p1 + t_p2 + t_w2
        midplane = L_grip / 2.0
        E_w2, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T)
        
        # Top-down slice profiles
        w1_end = min(t_w1, midplane)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, w1_end, d_w, d_h, E_w1)
        if midplane > t_w1:
            p1_end = min(t_w1 + t_p1, midplane)
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1, p1_end, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
            
        # Bottom-up slice profiles
        w2_end = min(t_w2, midplane)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, w2_end, d_w, d_h, E_w2)
        if midplane > t_w2:
            p2_end = min(t_w2 + t_p2, midplane)
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w2, p2_end, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
            
        # Cross-midplane sliver check
        if midplane > (t_w2 + t_p2):
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w2 + t_p2, midplane, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
        elif midplane > (t_w1 + t_p1):
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1 + t_p1, midplane, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
            
    return 1.0 / compliance

def get_bolt_stiffness(geom, T):
    """Calculates bolt tension stiffness matching the current configurations."""
    E_bolt, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T)
    A_bolt = np.pi * (geom['d_bolt']**2) / 4.0
    L_grip = get_grip_length(geom)
    return (A_bolt * E_bolt) / L_grip







Code
def analyze_cryo_joint_universal(geom, F_preload, T_start=293.15, T_end=4.0, steps=100):
    temperatures = np.linspace(T_start, T_end, steps)
    
    results = {
        'T': temperatures, 'force': [], 'k_b': [], 'k_m': [],
        'dL_members_total': [], 'dL_bolt_total': []
    }
    
    L_grip_ref = get_grip_length(geom)
    
    _, dL_b_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T_start)
    _, dL_w1_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T_start)
    _, dL_p1_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T_start)
    _, dL_p2_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T_start)
    
    # Safe decoupled check to prevent referencing non-unpacked nested values
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() != 'blind':
        _, dL_w2_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T_start)
    else:
        dL_w2_ref = 0.0
    
    for T in temperatures:
        k_b = get_bolt_stiffness(geom, T)
        k_m = get_member_stiffness(geom, T)
        
        _, dL_b = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T)
        _, dL_w1 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T)
        _, dL_p1 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T)
        _, dL_p2 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T)
        
        dl_w1_val = geom['t_w1'] * (dL_w1 - dL_w1_ref)
        dl_p1_val = geom['t_p1'] * (dL_p1 - dL_p1_ref)
        
        if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
            dl_p2_val = (0.5 * geom['L_eng']) * (dL_p2 - dL_p2_ref)
            dl_members_sum = dl_w1_val + dl_p1_val + dl_p2_val
        else:
            _, dL_w2 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T)
            dl_p2_val = geom['t_p2'] * (dL_p2 - dL_p2_ref)
            dl_w2_val = geom['t_w2'] * (dL_w2 - dL_w2_ref)
            dl_members_sum = dl_w1_val + dl_p1_val + dl_p2_val + dl_w2_val
            
        dl_bolt_sum = L_grip_ref * (dL_b - dL_b_ref)
        delta_F = (k_b * k_m / (k_b + k_m)) * (dl_members_sum - dl_bolt_sum)
        
        results['force'].append(F_preload + delta_F)
        results['k_b'].append(k_b)
        results['k_m'].append(k_m)
        results['dL_members_total'].append(dl_members_sum)
        results['dL_bolt_total'].append(dl_bolt_sum)
        
    for k in results.keys():
        if k != 'T': results[k] = np.array(results[k])
    return results

def calculate_frustum_stiffness(z1, z2, d_w, d_h, E, alpha_deg=30.0):
    """Computes stiffness for an isolated member frustum layer according to Shigley."""
    if np.isclose(z1, z2): return float('inf')
    alpha = np.radians(alpha_deg)
    tan_a = np.tan(alpha)
    num = (2 * z2 * tan_a + d_w - d_h) * (2 * z1 * tan_a + d_w + d_h)
    den = (2 * z2 * tan_a + d_w + d_h) * (2 * z1 * tan_a + d_w - d_h)
    return (np.pi * E * d_h * tan_a) / np.log(num / den)

def get_grip_length(geom):
    """Helper to find total physical clamp height based on joint type architecture."""
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
        return geom['t_w1'] + geom['t_p1'] + (0.5 * geom['L_eng'])
    else:
        return geom['t_w1'] + geom['t_p1'] + geom['t_p2'] + geom.get('t_w2', 0.0)

def get_member_stiffness(geom, T):
    """Dispatches stiffness stack tracking based on specified structural boundaries."""
    d_w, d_h = geom['d_w'], geom['d_h']
    t_w1, t_p1 = geom['t_w1'], geom['t_p1']
    
    E_w1, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T)
    E_p1, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T)
    E_p2, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T)
    
    compliance = 0.0
    
    # --- CONFIGURATION A: BLIND TAPPED HOLE ---
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
        t_p2_eff = 0.5 * geom['L_eng']
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, t_w1, d_w, d_h, E_w1)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1, t_w1 + t_p1, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1 + t_p1, t_w1 + t_p1 + t_p2_eff, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
        
    # --- CONFIGURATION B: THROUGH-BOLT & NUT ---
    else:
        t_w2, t_p2 = geom.get('t_w2', 0.0), geom['t_p2']
        L_grip = t_w1 + t_p1 + t_p2 + t_w2
        midplane = L_grip / 2.0
        E_w2, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T)
        
        # Top-down slice profiles
        w1_end = min(t_w1, midplane)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, w1_end, d_w, d_h, E_w1)
        if midplane > t_w1:
            p1_end = min(t_w1 + t_p1, midplane)
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1, p1_end, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
            
        # Bottom-up slice profiles
        w2_end = min(t_w2, midplane)
        compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(0, w2_end, d_w, d_h, E_w2)
        if midplane > t_w2:
            p2_end = min(t_w2 + t_p2, midplane)
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w2, p2_end, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
            
        # Cross-midplane sliver check
        if midplane > (t_w2 + t_p2):
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w2 + t_p2, midplane, d_w, d_h, E_p1)
        elif midplane > (t_w1 + t_p1):
            compliance += 1.0 / calculate_frustum_stiffness(t_w1 + t_p1, midplane, d_w, d_h, E_p2)
            
    return 1.0 / compliance

def get_bolt_stiffness(geom, T):
    """Calculates bolt tension stiffness matching the current configurations."""
    E_bolt, _ = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T)
    A_bolt = np.pi * (geom['d_bolt']**2) / 4.0
    L_grip = get_grip_length(geom)
    return (A_bolt * E_bolt) / L_grip

def analyze_cryo_joint_universal(geom, F_preload, T_start=293.15, T_end=4.0, steps=100):
    temperatures = np.linspace(T_start, T_end, steps)
    
    results = {
        'T': temperatures, 'force': [], 'k_b': [], 'k_m': [],
        'dL_members_total': [], 'dL_bolt_total': []
    }
    
    L_grip_ref = get_grip_length(geom)
    
    _, dL_b_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T_start)
    _, dL_w1_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T_start)
    _, dL_p1_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T_start)
    _, dL_p2_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T_start)
    
    # Safe decoupled check to prevent referencing non-unpacked nested values
    if geom['joint_type'].lower() != 'blind':
        _, dL_w2_ref = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T_start)
    else:
        dL_w2_ref = 0.0
    
    for T in temperatures:
        k_b = get_bolt_stiffness(geom, T)
        k_m = get_member_stiffness(geom, T)
        
        _, dL_b = get_material_properties(geom['mat_bolt'], T)
        _, dL_w1 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w1'], T)
        _, dL_p1 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p1'], T)
        _, dL_p2 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_p2'], T)
        
        dl_w1_val = geom['t_w1'] * (dL_w1 - dL_w1_ref)
        dl_p1_val = geom['t_p1'] * (dL_p1 - dL_p1_ref)
        
        if geom['joint_type'].lower() == 'blind':
            dl_p2_val = (0.5 * geom['L_eng']) * (dL_p2 - dL_p2_ref)
            dl_members_sum = dl_w1_val + dl_p1_val + dl_p2_val
        else:
            _, dL_w2 = get_material_properties(geom['mat_w2'], T)
            dl_p2_val = geom['t_p2'] * (dL_p2 - dL_p2_ref)
            dl_w2_val = geom['t_w2'] * (dL_w2 - dL_w2_ref)
            dl_members_sum = dl_w1_val + dl_p1_val + dl_p2_val + dl_w2_val
            
        dl_bolt_sum = L_grip_ref * (dL_b - dL_b_ref)
        delta_F = (k_b * k_m / (k_b + k_m)) * (dl_members_sum - dl_bolt_sum)
        
        results['force'].append(F_preload + delta_F)
        results['k_b'].append(k_b)
        results['k_m'].append(k_m)
        results['dL_members_total'].append(dl_members_sum)
        results['dL_bolt_total'].append(dl_bolt_sum)
        
    for k in results.keys():
        if k != 'T': results[k] = np.array(results[k])
    return results

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text: Once upon a time I got tired of tweaking my bbq dampers every hour for long smokes of brisket or pork shoulder. I put together an Arduino based PID fan controller that provided air flow from the bottom of the bbq, and I choked down the top damper. One challenge with this setup was reading out the temperature from a thermistor since most food probe thermometers are thermistors, not thermocouples.

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
Thermistor calibration
To calibrate the thermistor I filled a small pot with oil, and used a thermapen (food thermometer) and Fluke K type thermocouple as reference thermometers. I turned the burner on the lowest setting, continuously stirred the oil and moved the three thermometers (thermistor = unknown, thermapen, thermocouple) continuously to get an average of the oil bath temperature. The data and fit equation (Steinhart-Hart) are shown below. The Steinhart-Hart model predicts the temperature dependent resistance of a semiconductor, and is commonly used in industrial control and experimental measurements.
\[1/T = (a + b \cdot log(R) + c \cdot (log(R))^3)\]
All units are converted to Kelvin and Ohms before fitting. The error bars are estimated at $$2 degF and 0.5% of resistance reading + the least significant digit.
This fit curve was uesd in the Arduino to calculate the temperature of the thermistor probes.


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

# 1. Define fit curve function
def custom_curve(x, a, b, c):
    return (a+b*np.log(x)+c*(np.log(x))**3)

# 2. Read the CSV file
df = pd.read_csv("Thermistor-Oil.csv")

# Extract the X and Y columns and convert to Kelvin and Ohms
T_data = (df["BGE temp (F)"].values-32)*(5/9)+273.15
R_data = df["Thermistor (kOhm)"].values*1000

# Add error terms
# Fluke error is 0.5% of reading + least significant digit
R_error = 0.005*R_data + 1000
# Temperature error is assumed to be 2F, converted to Kelvin
T_error = 2*(5/9)

# 3. Fit the curve to the data
# curve_fit returns:
#   popt: Optimized parameters (a, b, c)
#   pcov: Covariance matrix (used to calculate parameter errors)
p0_guess = [1.1e-3, 2.3e-4, 8.7e-8]
bounds = (0, [1e-1, 1e-2, 1e-5]) 

popt, pcov = curve_fit(custom_curve, R_data, 1./T_data, p0=p0_guess, bounds=bounds)

# Print the fitted parameters
print("Fitted parameters:")
print(f"a = {popt[0]}")
print(f"b = {popt[1]}")
print(f"c = {popt[2]}")

# 4. Plot the original data and the fitted curve
# plt.scatter(T_data, R_data, color="red", label="Data")
plt.errorbar((T_data-273.15)*(9/5)+32, R_data/1000, yerr=R_error/1000, xerr=T_error, fmt='o', color="red", label="Data", ms=2, capsize=4)

# Generate smooth resistance values for the curve line
R_fit = np.linspace(min(R_data), max(R_data), 100)
T_fit = (1/custom_curve(R_fit, *popt) - 273.15)*(9/5)+32 # *popt unpacks the optimized a, b, c

plt.plot(T_fit, R_fit/1000, color="blue", label="Fitted Curve")
plt.xlabel("Temperature (degF)")
plt.ylabel("Resistance (kOhm)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()


Fitted parameters:
a = 0.0006879104473030154
b = 0.00017389502714043695
c = 1.0273748450819405e-07

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
BBQ Setup
The second part of this setup was programming the Arduino with PID control which is pretty straight forward with existing libraries. The control box was built with the fan internal to the box, which is shown below. The fan is trapped in a compartment on the left side of the box to transition from the fan housing to the tubing. The intake to the fan is on the external side of the box, not shown in the photo. The display in the box is for realtime temperature and fan speed control readout, and the second board in addition to the Arduino is a motor controller board to provide the higher currents that the fan motor needs.

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
BBQ In Action!
The image below shows the BBQ output and stability. The setpoint for the first portion of the cook was 225F and then it was increased to 300F after 9.75 hours because I got impatient. The black data is the grill temperature, the blue is the food probe, and the red is the fan percentage of power. The fan power is shifted on the plot to be between 100 and 200.
It took a couple of runs to get the PID parameters tuned, but ulitimately was quite stable, meaning I no longer had to baby-sit the bbq for long cooks.

In the data above I am using pulse width modulated motor control for the fan, but ran into issues with the fan being oversized. Many of the runs required such low fan speeds that the fan wouldn’t even spin up. To overcome this, I switched to ON/OFF control with an integration window. I implemented this by converting the PWM signal to a fan run time signal in a 5 or 10 second window. So a 10% PWM signal in a 10 second window means the fan would turn on for 1 second and turn off for the remaining 9 seconds. This worked very well, but ultimately killed the fan because of the constant inrush current needed to start the fan every 5-10 seconds. The smarter solution would have been to find the appropriately sized fan, and you’ll notice that some of the existing fan controlled bbq units on the market now use small fans, on the order of 2” in diameter.
While hunting for a smaller fan a few years later I noticed the SMOBOT controller. From a longevity perspective this is much better design than the active fan control I had implemented. This new controller also allowed for remote internet connections so I could get feedback from the BBQ while away from the house. This SMOBOT controller has worked so well over the last 7 years that I finally disassembled the Arduino model I made.

title: Engineering Projects
text: This website is a collection of engineering projects, home projects, calculations, and analysis. I would like to build out a site where I can access common technical knowledge. In my line of work, diverse technical projects tend to be lumped into handfuls of months or years as projects shift around. And by that I mean shifting between, solid mechanics, heat transfer (10’s of milliKelvin to 1000C), high vacuum systems, gas permeation problems, gas chemistry/adsorption, radiation transport, germanium detector design, gas proportional counter construction, material science of metals (oxidation/reduction, brazing, creep, thermal conductivity, etc.), electroplating, et-cetera. Recently I find myself digging up project work from 5-10 years prior, and trying to remember why we made the decisions at the time.
